Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A method and system for monitoring fluid flow in an open channel system, using an optical fibre that extends along at least a portion of the open channel system within the channel below the surface of the fluid. The method comprising sending light pulses into the sensor optical fibre, receiving backscattered light from the sensor optical fibre, and analysing properties of the backscattered light to obtain data representing strain along the sensor fibre. The strain data can be processed to derive information about the fluid flow, such as fluid depth, flow velocity and flow volume. A containment system for the optical fibre sensor may be included to protect the fibre and convert the pressure of a fluid in the open channel to a strain in the fibre. The temperature of the fluid may also be measured and temperature compensation of the measured strain carried out. The system is particularly applicable to sewers, drains, culverts or levees, with the optical fibre sensor installed axially at the bottom of the channel.

outputs.L3:
The method monitors fluid flow in an open channel by using an optical fibre positioned below the surface of the fluid along at least part of the channel. The optical fibre is arranged so that it extends through or alongside the region in which the flow is to be measured, enabling measurements to be taken at multiple points along its length.

In operation, light pulses are transmitted through the optical fibre. As the pulses travel along the fibre, a portion of the light is backscattered. This backscattered light is analysed to obtain strain data at different locations along the fibre. Because the fibre is exposed, directly or indirectly, to forces associated with the surrounding fluid, changes in strain can be related to changes in the flow conditions within the channel.

The strain data may then be processed to determine one or more characteristics of the fluid flow. These characteristics may include the depth of the fluid, the velocity of the flow, and the volume or volumetric flow rate passing through the channel. By analysing how strain varies along the optical fibre and over time, the system can provide distributed monitoring rather than relying on a single measurement point.

In some implementations, the optical fibre may be housed within a containment system. The containment system can protect the fibre from damage caused by debris, abrasion, chemical exposure, or other environmental conditions. It may also be configured to transfer or convert pressure exerted by the fluid into measurable strain in the optical fibre, thereby improving the reliability and sensitivity of the measurements.

The system may also be used to measure fluid temperature, for example by analysing temperature-dependent changes in the optical signal. This allows both hydraulic and thermal conditions to be monitored using the same fibre-based sensing arrangement.

The method is particularly suitable for use in open-channel environments such as sewers, stormwater drains, culverts, irrigation channels, and levees. In these settings, the distributed nature of the optical fibre sensing system can provide continuous or near-continuous information about flow behaviour, supporting monitoring, maintenance, flood management, and infrastructure assessment.
outputs.L4:
The system is designed to monitor the flow of fluid in an open channel, such as a sewer, storm drain, culvert, irrigation channel, drainage ditch, or levee-related waterway. It uses an optical fibre sensor positioned along or within the channel so that at least part of the fibre is located below the surface of the flowing fluid. By using the fibre itself as a distributed sensing element, the system can obtain measurements over a length of the channel rather than only at a single point.

In operation, pulses of light are transmitted into the optical fibre. As the light travels along the fibre, a portion of it is naturally backscattered. The system receives and analyzes this backscattered light to determine strain at different locations along the fibre. Because the fibre is exposed to forces associated with the surrounding fluid, changes in strain can be related to conditions in the channel.

The measured strain data can be processed to determine characteristics of the fluid flow. For example, the strain experienced by the fibre may indicate the depth of fluid above or around the fibre. Variations in strain over time and along the length of the fibre may also be used to estimate flow velocity. From the depth and velocity information, the system can further calculate fluid volume or volumetric flow rate through the channel.

The optical fibre may be installed directly in the channel or may be incorporated into a protective structure to prevent damage from debris, abrasion, chemical exposure, or high flow conditions. In some implementations, the fibre may be coupled to a pressure-responsive element that converts pressure from the fluid into strain in the fibre, improving the ability to infer fluid depth or hydraulic loading. The system may also include temperature compensation, since temperature changes can affect optical fibre measurements and may otherwise be mistaken for strain caused by fluid flow.

By providing distributed, real-time or near-real-time measurements, the system can help monitor changing hydraulic conditions across long sections of infrastructure. It is particularly useful in environments where conventional point sensors may be difficult to install, maintain, or protect. Potential applications include wastewater networks, stormwater systems, culverts, open drains, flood-control channels, and levees, where information about water depth, flow velocity, and total flow volume can support maintenance, flood prediction, capacity planning, and structural safety monitoring.

**The**

“The” is one of the most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in making meaning clear. It is called the definite article because it points to a specific person, place, thing, or idea. For example, “a book” could mean any book, but “the book” refers to a particular book that the speaker and listener understand.

This small word helps create precision in communication. When someone says “the sun,” we know they are talking about the star at the center of our solar system. When a teacher says “open the door,” the listener usually knows which door is meant. Without “the,” many sentences would sound incomplete or unclear.

“The” is also flexible. It can be used with singular nouns, plural nouns, and uncountable nouns: “the car,” “the children,” and “the water.” Although it is short and simple, it appears constantly in speech and writing, quietly connecting ideas and guiding understanding.

In many ways, “the” shows how powerful small words can be. It may not carry much meaning on its own, but in a sentence, it helps define, identify, and organize the world around us.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a method and system for measuring depth, velocity, and volume of fluid flow in an open channel using backscattered light from an optical fibre installed along the channel bottom.
counterfactuals.output:
A method/system is described for measuring open-channel flow using an optical fibre installed lengthwise along the channel bottom.

The system launches light into the fibre and analyzes light backscattered from different points along the fibre, allowing the fibre to act as a distributed sensor. Fluid flowing over the fibre causes local mechanical/thermal disturbances, such as pressure fluctuations, vibration, strain, or temperature changes, which alter the backscattered optical signal. By time- or frequency-resolving the returned light, the system determines where along the channel these disturbances occur and how they vary with time.

From the backscatter data, the system estimates:

- **Flow depth:** inferred from the portion of the bottom-mounted fibre that is wetted or from pressure/temperature/strain signatures associated with water coverage.
- **Flow velocity:** determined by tracking moving turbulence, waves, or flow-induced disturbance patterns along the fibre, often using correlation between signals at spaced fibre locations.
- **Flow volume/flow rate:** calculated by combining measured depth with channel geometry to obtain cross-sectional flow area, and multiplying by the measured velocity.

The system may include an optical interrogator, laser/source, photodetector, signal processor, and a fibre-optic cable protected or embedded along the channel bed. Because sensing is distributed along the fibre, the approach can measure spatially varying flow conditions without installing many separate point sensors in the channel.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical overview of an optical fibre sensor system placed below the fluid surface in drains or levees to derive strain data and infer flow characteristics, including temperature compensation.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Overview: Submerged Optical Fibre Sensor System for Strain-Based Flow Monitoring in Drains and Levees

### 1. System Purpose

The proposed system uses optical fibre sensing elements installed below the fluid surface in drains, levees, culverts, or seepage channels to measure strain induced by hydraulic loading and flow interaction. By continuously monitoring strain along or at discrete points of the fibre, the system can infer flow-related characteristics such as water level changes, flow velocity trends, turbulence, seepage activity, and structural deformation.

Because optical fibres are also sensitive to temperature, the system incorporates temperature compensation to separate true mechanical strain from thermally induced wavelength or phase shifts.

---

### 2. Operating Principle

Optical fibre sensors detect changes in light transmission caused by mechanical deformation, pressure, vibration, or temperature variation along the fibre. When the fibre is bonded to, embedded in, or tensioned across a submerged structure, changes in hydraulic forces alter the strain state of the fibre.

Typical sensing approaches include:

- **Fibre Bragg Grating sensors**, or FBGs, for discrete strain and temperature measurements.
- **Distributed Acoustic Sensing**, or DAS, for vibration and dynamic strain over long distances.
- **Distributed Temperature and Strain Sensing**, or DTSS, using Brillouin or Rayleigh scattering for spatially distributed measurements.
- **Interferometric fibre sensors** for high-sensitivity local strain or pressure detection.

In an FBG-based system, a grating written into the fibre reflects a narrow wavelength band. Strain or temperature changes shift the reflected wavelength. The measured wavelength shift is then converted into strain after temperature correction.

---

### 3. System Configuration

A typical submerged installation includes the following components:

1. **Optical fibre sensing cable**
   - Installed below the normal fluid surface.
   - Mounted along the invert of a drain, sidewall of a channel, internal face of a levee drain, or within a seepage collection trench.
   - May be bonded, clamped, embedded in geotextile, or mounted on a flexible carrier beam.

2. **Strain-sensing sections**
   - Regions of fibre coupled mechanically to the surrounding structure or hydraulic interface.
   - Designed to respond to bending, tensile strain, vibration, or pressure-induced deformation.

3. **Temperature reference sensors**
   - Either separate temperature-only FBGs isolated from mechanical strain, or a parallel fibre that is thermally coupled but mechanically decoupled.
   - Used to remove thermal effects from strain measurements.

4. **Optical interrogator**
   - Launches light into the fibre and records wavelength shifts, backscatter phase changes, or intensity variations.
   - Located above water level in a protected cabinet or control room.
   - Connected to the sensing cable through ruggedized optical leads.

5. **Data acquisition and processing unit**
   - Converts optical measurements into strain, temperature, vibration, or pressure-derived values.
   - Applies filtering, calibration curves, and flow inference models.

6. **Communications and power**
   - May use mains, solar, battery, or hybrid power.
   - Data can be transmitted by cellular, radio, fibre backhaul, Ethernet, or satellite link.

---

### 4. Installation Below the Fluid Surface

The fibre sensor is placed below the water or fluid surface to ensure direct coupling to hydraulic effects. Depending on the monitoring objective, the cable may be installed in one of several ways:

- **Along the bed of a drain or channel**, where flow-induced drag, sediment movement, and hydraulic pressure fluctuations create measurable strain or vibration.
- **On a submerged structural member**, such as a plate, rod, beam, or membrane, where flow causes deflection that is transferred to the fibre.
- **Across a seepage path or outlet**, where increased seepage produces changes in vibration, bending, or local deformation.
- **Embedded in the levee body or drainage layer**, where pore-pressure changes and seepage-induced deformation alter the strain profile.
- **Mounted vertically or diagonally**, allowing changes in water level to be inferred from differential pressure-induced bending or from wet/dry thermal behaviour.

The cable jacket and attachment method must be selected for long-term immersion, abrasion resistance, chemical compatibility, and resistance to biological fouling.

---

### 5. Strain Measurement

The measured optical response is converted into strain using calibration constants for the sensing fibre.

For an FBG sensor, the reflected wavelength shift can be represented as:

\[
\Delta \lambda_B = K_\varepsilon \Delta \varepsilon + K_T \Delta T
\]

where:

- \(\Delta \lambda_B\) is the measured Bragg wavelength shift,
- \(K_\varepsilon\) is the strain sensitivity coefficient,
- \(\Delta \varepsilon\) is the mechanical strain change,
- \(K_T\) is the temperature sensitivity coefficient,
- \(\Delta T\) is the temperature change.

After temperature compensation, the mechanical strain is:

\[
\Delta \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta \lambda_B - K_T \Delta T}{K_\varepsilon}
\]

For distributed sensing systems, the same principle applies, but the measurement is resolved continuously along the fibre length rather than at discrete grating points.

---

### 6. Temperature Compensation

Temperature compensation is essential because submerged environments can experience gradual thermal variation, solar heating, stormwater inflow temperature differences, groundwater exchange, and seasonal shifts.

Common compensation methods include:

#### 6.1 Mechanically Isolated Temperature Sensors

A temperature-only optical sensor is placed close to each strain sensor but isolated from mechanical strain. It experiences the same fluid temperature as the strain sensor but does not respond to structural deformation.

The temperature measurement is used to correct the strain sensor reading.

#### 6.2 Paired FBG Configuration

Two gratings are installed near each other:

- One bonded to the structure or sensing element and responsive to strain plus temperature.
- One housed in a loose tube or capillary, responsive only to temperature.

The compensated strain is obtained by subtracting the temperature-induced wavelength shift measured by the reference grating.

#### 6.3 Dual-Fibre Distributed Compensation

For distributed systems, one fibre may be mechanically coupled to the drain or levee structure, while a second parallel fibre is mechanically decoupled but thermally coupled to the same environment. The distributed temperature profile from the reference fibre is used to correct the distributed strain profile.

#### 6.4 Model-Based Compensation

Where direct reference sensors are limited, thermal effects can be estimated using known thermal expansion coefficients, historical baseline data, fluid temperature probes, and environmental models. This is less robust than direct temperature measurement but may be useful as a secondary correction.

---

### 7. Inferring Flow Characteristics

The fibre system does not necessarily measure flow directly; instead, it measures strain, vibration, or pressure-induced deformation correlated with hydraulic conditions. Flow characteristics are inferred through calibration and signal processing.

#### 7.1 Flow Rate and Velocity

Flow velocity can be inferred from:

- Drag-induced strain on a submerged sensing element.
- Deflection of a cantilevered or tensioned fibre carrier.
- Turbulence-induced vibration frequency and amplitude.
- Distributed strain gradients along the channel.

For a calibrated flexible element exposed to flow, drag force is approximately related to velocity by:

\[
F_D = \frac{1}{2} \rho C_D A v^2
\]

where:

- \(F_D\) is drag force,
- \(\rho\) is fluid density,
- \(C_D\) is drag coefficient,
- \(A\) is projected area,
- \(v\) is flow velocity.

If the drag force creates measurable strain in the fibre-mounted element, velocity can be estimated after calibration.

#### 7.2 Water Level or Hydraulic Head

Water level may be inferred from:

- Hydrostatic pressure-induced deformation of a membrane or beam.
- Vertical arrays of strain sensors.
- Distributed strain changes along submerged portions of the cable.
- Temperature contrast between air-exposed and submerged fibre sections.

Hydrostatic pressure follows:

\[
p = \rho g h
\]

where:

- \(p\) is pressure,
- \(\rho\) is fluid density,
- \(g\) is gravitational acceleration,
- \(h\) is fluid depth.

A pressure-sensitive fibre carrier can translate this pressure into strain.

#### 7.3 Turbulence and Flow Regime

Dynamic strain or acoustic signals can indicate:

- Laminar-to-turbulent transition,
- Blockage or debris accumulation,
- Sediment transport,
- Vortex shedding,
- Pump or gate operation,
- Rapid inflow during storm events.

Spectral analysis of the strain signal can identify dominant vibration frequencies and energy bands associated with specific hydraulic behaviours.

#### 7.4 Seepage and Internal Erosion in Levees

In levee applications, the submerged fibre may detect:

- Localized seepage increases,
- Piping initiation,
- Internal erosion,
- Settlement or deformation,
- Crack opening,
- Changes in pore pressure or hydraulic gradient.

Distributed strain anomalies, especially when correlated with temperature anomalies caused by seepage flow, can provide early warning of developing instability.

---

### 8. Data Processing Workflow

A typical processing sequence is:

1. **Acquire optical measurements**
   - FBG wavelength shifts, backscatter strain profiles, or acoustic phase data.

2. **Synchronize temperature readings**
   - Use colocated temperature sensors or reference fibre.

3. **Apply temperature compensation**
   - Remove thermal strain effects from the raw signal.

4. **Convert optical response to mechanical strain**
   - Use calibration coefficients and sensor-specific sensitivity factors.

5. **Filter and condition data**
   - Remove noise, drift, and outliers.
   - Separate quasi-static strain from dynamic vibration components.

6. **Extract hydraulic indicators**
   - Strain amplitude,
   - Strain gradient,
   - Frequency spectrum,
   - Event duration,
   - Rate of change,
   - Spatial anomaly location.

7. **Infer flow conditions**
   - Apply empirical calibration curves, physics-based models, or machine-learning regression.

8. **Generate alerts**
   - Trigger alarms for abnormal flow, blockage, scour, seepage increase, or levee deformation.

---

### 9. Calibration Requirements

Accurate flow inference requires calibration under known hydraulic conditions. Calibration may include:

- Laboratory flume testing,
- Controlled discharge testing in the field,
- Comparison with conventional flow meters,
- Water level gauge correlation,
- Pressure transducer comparison,
- Temperature chamber calibration,
- Mechanical strain calibration of the fibre attachment.

Calibration establishes relationships between compensated strain and hydraulic variables such as velocity, discharge, pressure, or water level.

Long-term installations should include periodic validation to account for fouling, sediment deposition, cable relaxation, structural changes, and sensor aging.

---

### 10. Design Considerations

Important design parameters include:

- **Sensor type:** FBG, DAS, Brillouin, Rayleigh, or hybrid.
- **Spatial resolution:** Point sensing versus distributed sensing.
- **Sampling rate:** Slow quasi-static seepage monitoring versus high-rate turbulence or vibration monitoring.
- **Cable protection:** Armoured, abrasion-resistant, chemically compatible jackets.
- **Mechanical coupling:** Adequate strain transfer without overstressing the fibre.
- **Biofouling and sedimentation:** Protective housings or self-cleaning placement may be required.
- **Redundancy:** Multiple fibres or sensor paths improve reliability.
- **Ingress protection:** Interrogator and splice enclosures must be above flood level or sealed appropriately.
- **Baseline stability:** Initial readings should be established over varying thermal and hydraulic conditions.
- **Maintainability:** Sensor routing should allow inspection or replacement where practical.

---

### 11. Advantages

Optical fibre sensing offers several benefits for submerged drain and levee monitoring:

- Immune to electromagnetic interference,
- Suitable for long-distance monitoring,
- Can provide distributed measurements over many metres or kilometres,
- Passive sensing element with no electrical power in the water,
- High sensitivity to small strain changes,
- Compatible with harsh or wet environments,
- Can combine strain, vibration, and temperature sensing in one system,
- Useful for early detection of abnormal hydraulic or structural behaviour.

---

### 12. Limitations

Potential limitations include:

- Flow is inferred indirectly and requires calibration,
- Temperature effects must be carefully compensated,
- Mechanical coupling strongly affects measurement quality,
- Sensor response may change due to sediment, debris, or biofouling,
- Installation damage can affect optical continuity,
- Data interpretation may be site-specific,
- High-performance interrogators can be costly.

---

### 13. Summary

A submerged optical fibre sensor system can provide continuous strain-based monitoring of drains, levees, and seepage pathways. By placing the sensing fibre below the fluid surface and mechanically coupling it to hydraulic forces or structural deformation, the system captures strain and vibration signatures related to flow conditions. Temperature compensation, using mechanically isolated reference sensors or distributed thermal reference fibres, is required to distinguish mechanical strain from thermal effects.

With appropriate calibration and signal processing, compensated strain data can be used to infer water level, flow velocity trends, discharge changes, turbulence, blockage, seepage, and levee deformation. The result is a robust, passive, and scalable monitoring approach suitable for civil infrastructure, flood defence, drainage systems, and geotechnical risk management.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an invention summary for a protected fibre optic sensor in an open channel that converts fluid pressure into fibre strain and analyzes reflected light pulses to monitor flow.
counterfactuals.output:
## Invention Summary

The invention relates to a protected fibre optic flow sensor for use in an open channel, such as a drainage channel, irrigation canal, sewer conduit, flume, or other partially filled fluid passage. The sensor converts fluid pressure acting on a protected sensing element into strain in an optical fibre, and determines flow-related parameters by analyzing reflected optical light pulses transmitted through the fibre.

In one embodiment, the sensor includes an optical fibre arranged within or coupled to a pressure-responsive structure positioned in the open channel. The pressure-responsive structure may include a diaphragm, membrane, tube, plate, chamber, or other deformable member that is exposed to hydrostatic and/or dynamic pressure from the flowing fluid. As the fluid level or flow condition changes, the pressure-responsive structure deflects or deforms, thereby inducing strain in the optical fibre.

The optical fibre is protected from direct contact with debris, sediment, chemical attack, abrasion, and mechanical impact by a protective housing, coating, conduit, or encapsulation. The protective structure allows pressure transmission to the sensing element while shielding the fibre from damage in harsh open-channel environments.

Light pulses are launched into the optical fibre from an interrogation unit. Reflections from fibre sensing regions, such as fibre Bragg gratings, Rayleigh backscatter regions, reflective markers, or other optical discontinuities, are returned to the interrogation unit. Changes in the reflected light, including wavelength shift, phase shift, intensity variation, time-of-flight variation, or backscatter signature, are analyzed to determine strain in the fibre. The measured strain is correlated with fluid pressure, fluid level, velocity, or flow rate in the open channel.

The system may include temperature compensation, calibration data, signal processing algorithms, and flow conversion models to translate fibre strain measurements into real-time flow monitoring information. Multiple sensing regions may be provided along the fibre to measure pressure or level at different locations, enabling distributed or multi-point monitoring.

The invention provides a robust, electrically passive, corrosion-resistant, and remotely interrogated sensor suitable for long-term deployment in open-channel flow environments. Because the sensing fibre contains no electrical components at the measurement location, the system is well suited for wet, corrosive, explosive, or difficult-to-access installations.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe, in patent language, a system for monitoring sewer or culvert flow using an axial optical fibre sensor, including containment, strain analysis, and measurement of fluid depth and velocity.
counterfactuals.output:
A system for monitoring flow within a sewer, culvert, conduit, channel, or other hydraulic passage comprises an elongate optical fibre sensing element disposed generally axially with respect to a direction of fluid flow, a containment assembly configured to position and protect the sensing element within the passage, and an interrogation and processing unit configured to determine one or more hydraulic parameters from strain-induced optical responses of the sensing element.

In one embodiment, the optical fibre sensing element comprises a fibre Bragg grating array, a distributed acoustic sensing fibre, a distributed strain sensing fibre, a Rayleigh-scattering-based distributed sensing fibre, a Brillouin-based distributed sensing fibre, or any combination thereof. The sensing element extends along a longitudinal axis of the passage and is arranged such that flowing fluid imposes mechanical loading on the sensing element or on a carrier mechanically coupled to the sensing element. The optical fibre thereby produces a measurable optical response representative of axial strain, bending strain, vibration, fluctuating drag, hydrostatic loading, or other deformation caused by the surrounding fluid.

The containment assembly may comprise an elongate tube, sheath, rod, cable, beam, perforated conduit, slotted housing, or hydrodynamic carrier secured within the sewer or culvert. The containment assembly is configured to isolate the optical fibre from debris impact, abrasion, chemical attack, sediment transport, and direct mechanical damage while permitting pressure, drag, turbulence, buoyancy, or flow-induced vibration to be transferred to the fibre sensing element. The containment assembly may include one or more apertures, membranes, compliant sections, strain-transfer elements, pressure-transfer diaphragms, anchors, spacers, end mounts, or calibration features. In some embodiments the optical fibre is bonded, clamped, embedded, helically wrapped, or otherwise mechanically coupled to the containment assembly so that deformation of the containment assembly produces corresponding strain in the optical fibre.

The system further comprises a mounting arrangement for installing the containment assembly substantially parallel to the direction of flow, for example along an invert, sidewall, crown, or centerline of the sewer or culvert. The mounting arrangement may include brackets, standoffs, tensioning members, end anchors, weighted bases, magnetic fasteners, adhesive pads, expansion anchors, or resilient supports. The axial orientation enables spatially resolved sensing along the direction of flow, allowing the system to detect variations in fluid loading over a plurality of longitudinal positions.

An optical interrogator is optically coupled to the sensing element and configured to transmit optical energy into the fibre and receive reflected, backscattered, or transmitted optical signals. The interrogator determines strain, strain rate, vibration, temperature-compensated strain, or dynamic pressure-related signals at a plurality of sensing locations along the optical fibre. The interrogator may be located remotely from the sewer or culvert and connected by a lead fibre, thereby permitting operation in hazardous or inaccessible environments.

A processor receives data from the interrogator and performs strain analysis to derive hydraulic measurements. The processor may compare measured strain profiles with stored calibration data, analytical models, finite-element models, empirical transfer functions, or machine-learning models correlating fibre strain with fluid depth, velocity, discharge, surcharge condition, blockage, sediment accumulation, or flow regime. The processor may separate quasi-static strain components associated with hydrostatic pressure or buoyancy from dynamic strain components associated with turbulence, vortex shedding, drag fluctuations, wave action, or debris passage.

Fluid depth may be determined by identifying a longitudinal or circumferential portion of the containment assembly subjected to wetting, hydrostatic pressure, buoyancy, temperature shift, or drag-induced strain. In one implementation, the depth of fluid above the containment assembly is inferred from a static or low-frequency strain component corresponding to hydrostatic pressure acting on a compliant portion of the containment assembly. In another implementation, depth is determined by detecting a transition between submerged and non-submerged fibre sections based on differences in thermal response, vibration damping, drag excitation, or strain offset. The processor converts the measured strain response into a fluid depth value using calibration coefficients associated with the geometry and stiffness of the containment assembly.

Fluid velocity may be determined from dynamic strain signatures generated by flow-induced loading on the axial sensing element. The processor may determine velocity from drag-related strain magnitude, vortex-shedding frequency, turbulence-induced vibration spectra, cross-correlation of strain fluctuations between spaced sensing locations, time-of-flight of coherent flow structures, or phase delay between strain signals measured at two or more longitudinal positions. In one embodiment, velocity is calculated by correlating dynamic strain signals at upstream and downstream fibre locations separated by a known distance and determining a convection time delay. In another embodiment, velocity is obtained from a calibrated relationship between flow speed and the amplitude or frequency content of axial strain induced in the containment assembly.

The system may further calculate volumetric flow rate by combining the measured fluid depth with the measured velocity and a known cross-sectional geometry of the sewer or culvert. The processor may compute wetted area as a function of depth and multiply the wetted area by an average velocity, optionally applying correction factors for velocity profile, roughness, slope, partial-pipe flow, surcharge flow, sediment level, or hydraulic radius.

The strain analysis may include temperature compensation using a reference fibre, an unstrained fibre segment, a protected grating, or distributed temperature measurements. The processor may filter noise, remove baseline drift, compensate for installation tension, detect sensor faults, and distinguish hydraulic strain from mechanical disturbances caused by maintenance activity, floating debris, rodents, traffic vibration, or structural movement.

In some embodiments, the containment assembly includes multiple sensing zones having different mechanical sensitivities. A first zone may be optimized for hydrostatic pressure or fluid-depth measurement, while a second zone is optimized for velocity measurement by drag or vibration response. The optical fibre may pass continuously through both zones, enabling depth and velocity measurements using a single fibre. Alternatively, multiple fibres or multiple fibre cores may be provided for redundancy, directional discrimination, temperature compensation, or independent measurement channels.

The system may include a communications module configured to transmit measured depth, velocity, discharge, alarm states, or diagnostic data to a remote monitoring station. The processor may generate alerts indicative of surcharge, backwater, blockage, excessive velocity, dry-weather infiltration, inflow during storm events, sediment buildup, or structural obstruction.

In claim-style form, the system may be characterized as follows:

1. A flow monitoring system for a sewer or culvert, comprising:  
   an optical fibre sensing element extending in an axial direction of a hydraulic passage;  
   a containment assembly housing or supporting the optical fibre sensing element and configured to transfer flow-induced mechanical loading to the optical fibre sensing element while protecting the optical fibre sensing element from debris and abrasion;  
   an optical interrogator optically coupled to the optical fibre sensing element and configured to obtain strain data from a plurality of locations along the optical fibre sensing element; and  
   a processor configured to analyze the strain data to determine both a depth of fluid in the hydraulic passage and a velocity of the fluid.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein the processor determines the depth of fluid from a static or quasi-static strain component corresponding to hydrostatic pressure, buoyancy, wetting, or damping of the containment assembly.

3. The system of claim 1, wherein the processor determines the velocity of the fluid from a dynamic strain component comprising one or more of drag-induced strain, flow-induced vibration, vortex-shedding frequency, turbulence spectra, or a time delay between strain signals measured at spaced axial locations.

4. The system of claim 1, wherein the containment assembly comprises an elongate protective member having one or more compliant portions, apertures, diaphragms, strain-transfer regions, or hydrodynamic surfaces configured to enhance sensitivity to fluid loading.

5. The system of claim 1, wherein the processor is further configured to calculate volumetric flow rate from the determined depth, the determined velocity, and a cross-sectional geometry of the sewer or culvert.

6. The system of claim 1, wherein the optical fibre sensing element comprises a distributed optical fibre sensor or an array of fibre Bragg gratings configured to provide spatially resolved strain measurement along the axial direction of the hydraulic passage.

Thus, the described arrangement provides a protected axial optical fibre sensor capable of monitoring hydraulic conditions in sewer and culvert environments by converting flow-induced mechanical effects into optical strain measurements and processing those measurements to derive fluid depth, velocity, and flow rate.
